items.summary: Travel plays a far more critical role in mental health and well-being than previously thought, according to new University of the Sunshine Coast-led research. items.summary: Scientists are getting a leg up on the rice stink bug, one of the most significant threats to rice, a staple food for nearly half the world's population and a major crop in Arkansas.

items.title: At-risk gamers gambling with their financial future
items.summary: Nearly 8 out of every 10 people at risk of gaming disorder have experienced overspending or financial harm due to their habit, an international study led by University of Queensland researchers found.

items.title: Birds basking in natural 'saunas'
items.summary: New research led by the University of Otago—Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka shows some bird species may be taking advantage of natural geothermal "health spas."

items.title: New livestream brings remote Australian arid zone waterhole to the world
items.summary: A new livestream from a remote waterhole in the Northern Territory is giving people around the world the opportunity to observe wildlife in real time.

items.title: Political boot camps for women could redress gender imbalance
items.summary: Immersive boot camps for women could be a way to overcome the stark gender imbalance in political leadership, according to new research that examined how to increase the political ambitions of talented women.

items.title: Cuttlefish suckers reveal how they grip rough prey—and could inspire better technology
items.summary: Cephalopods are a group of soft-bodied marine mollusks that include cuttlefish, octopuses, squid and nautiluses. Many of these mollusks have muscular suckers on their arms that allow them to seize prey or grip other surfaces in their surroundings.

items.title: Urban fire risk rises 30% in higher-income neighborhoods, analysis finds
items.summary: Frequently located on hillsides and in canyons surrounded by wildlands, wealthy neighborhoods are more likely to catch fire. However, a UC Riverside study shows they are also likely to recover faster than lower-income areas.

items.title: Dungeons & Dragons study rolls for better well-being
items.summary: Rolling dice and battling imaginary monsters might seem an unlikely source of well-being, but Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) research suggests Dungeons & Dragons groups can provide meaningful social connections and a strong sense of belonging.

items.summary: Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. items.title: World's water cycle becoming more unpredictable, UN warns
items.summary: The planet's water cycle is becoming increasingly erratic, swinging between too little and too much, the United Nations warned Thursday, with an unprecedented El Niño expected to exacerbate the long-term trend.

items.title: NASA spacecraft discovers a huge new crater on the moon
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.

items.title: Climate change made deadly Nepal glacier and rock collapse more likely, according to analysis
items.summary: Human-caused global warming thinned glaciers and thawed mountain permafrost, likely helping to destabilize the Himalayan slope that collapsed last month and unleashed catastrophic flooding across Nepal, according to a report released Thursday.

items.title: Does AI make us smarter or more dependent?
items.summary: Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming part of how people learn, solve problems and construct knowledge. Yet whether AI strengthens human intelligence or encourages excessive dependence remains an open question.
